Source: Proposition 1 text, Section 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1). The separate $1.25 billion veterans bond is in the Military and Veterans Code section of the same text (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
The Legislative Analyst estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds. It would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, buy or repair homes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The measure sets no production targets of its own (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No set share for the City. The bond money goes to state programs. The Legislative Analyst says the rental programs “generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Projects in Los Angeles would compete for it statewide. The analysis does not estimate how much would reach the City.
Money cities can apply for. $200 million would be “available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The text sends it through the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program, which requires a local trust fund with its own ongoing money (text, Sec. 54054(b)(11) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Stalled projects in the region. Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit housing lender that backs Proposition 1 and gave $100,000 to the Yes campaign, counted 39,880 affordable homes statewide that had local approvals but lacked the funding to start construction at the end of 2025. It put 9,533 of them in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. It did not break out the City of Los Angeles (Enterprise report, p. 3 (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf#page=3); Yes on Prop 1 coalition list (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition)).
The City’s own housing tax. The City’s main local source of new affordable housing money is Measure ULA, the tax on property sales over $5 million. The Housing Department reported it raised nearly $1.2 billion from its start through April 30, 2026 (LAHD report, May 10, 2026 (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-0088-S1_rpt_lahd_05-10-26.pdf)). The Legislative Analyst says Proposition 1 money “would be used together with other government monies” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)).
No City tax. The state would repay the $10 billion bond from its General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Proposition 1 does not create a local tax (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
We did not find a City Council resolution or City Housing Department statement on Proposition 1 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 1 is a bond act written by the Legislature. It needed a two-thirds vote in each house and the Governor’s signature, then voter approval (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI); SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Feb. 18, 2025: SB 417 was introduced (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). Its lead authors are Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas. The principal coauthors are Sen. Christopher Cabaldon and Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 6, 2026: The Senate Housing Committee approved it 8-1 (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 27, 2026: The Senate passed it 30-9. The no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Choi, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Niello, Seyarto, Strickland and Valladares (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
April 22 and May 14, 2026: The Assembly Housing Committee (10-2) and Appropriations Committee (12-3) approved it (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly passed the amended bill 61-7, the Senate agreed 29-2, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it the same day. It became Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026 (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). The Assembly no votes were Chen, DeMaio, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Seyarto and Strickland (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a state bond law cannot take effect until it has been submitted to the people and “shall have received a majority of all the votes cast for and against it at such election” (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI)). The bond act itself says it becomes operative only if voters adopt it on Nov. 3, 2026 (text, Sec. 54051 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 1 (November 2018): a $4 billion housing and veterans bond (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 56.2% statewide and 64.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)). The Budget Center says its money was fully committed by the end of 2023 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2018): $2 billion for supportive housing for people with mental illness (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 63.4% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 1 (March 2024): a mental health bond that included $2 billion for housing for veterans and others facing homelessness (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). It passed with 50.2% statewide and 54.0% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, March 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
The argument in favor is signed by Anni Chung of Self-Help for the Elderly, Jeffery Freitas of the California Federation of Teachers and John H. Ing of US Vets (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Need: “More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.”
Veterans: $1.25 billion goes “solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership” through CalVet.
Construction: it “jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes.”
Taxes and oversight: “NO NEW TAXES,” with public reporting, and it “unlocks federal matching funds.”
No argument against Proposition 1 was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Chione Flegal, executive director of Housing California, which backs the measure, told the Bay Area News Group that tens of thousands of affordable units are “shovel-ready” and that “you have both an incredible need and the conditions to actually get building quickly” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says “the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest” and that bonds used for programs rather than capital projects are “a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)). Spokesperson Susan Shelley said, “The more you pile this debt on, the more difficult the budget process is” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
State Sen. Tony Strickland, who voted no, told LAist the measure has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation,” and said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)).
California YIMBY supports it and estimates the production money could build about 43,700 affordable homes. It also says the $500 million in down payment help “could drive up home prices” if housing supply does not grow (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-1-2026/)).

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.
For help choosing where to trade ballot measures, compare election prediction apps (https://defirate.com/prediction-markets/politics/) for proposition coverage, fees and access.

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

Part of the Quadratín news network, Quadratín California provides Spanish-language coverage of issues affecting California and the binational community.

What does a yes vote on Proposition 1 mean?
The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 1 mean?
The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
What would Proposition 1 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would pay $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years to repay the $10 billion housing bond, about 0.25% of the state General Fund budget. The $1.25 billion veterans bond would be repaid by veterans' loan payments, which the Analyst says has always meant no direct state cost.
What it means for the City of LA
The City of Los Angeles would not receive a set share. The money goes through state competitive programs, mostly loans to developers and local governments for affordable rental housing. $200 million is set aside for local housing trust funds and local pilot programs. A 2026 Enterprise Community Partners study counted 9,533 stalled affordable homes in Los Angeles and Ventura counties waiting for public funding. The state would repay the bond from its General Fund, not from City taxes.
The details
Official title Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Type Legislative statute (general obligation bond), placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. The State Constitution (Article XVI, Section 1) says a state bond law takes effect only if it receives "a majority of all the votes cast for and against it."
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 1 on the March 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for mental health treatment facilities, which passed with 50.2% of the vote (Secretary of State, March 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 1 passes
State housing bond money The 2018 housing bond has been spent. The last voter-approved housing money was $2 billion in the 2024 mental health bond (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm); LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)) $10 billion in new general obligation bonds for housing programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Veterans home loans (CalVet) Last funded by a $1 billion bond in 2018 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)) $1.25 billion more, repaid by veterans’ mortgage payments (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
State budget About $6 billion a year goes to repay bonds, about 3% of General Fund revenue (LAO bond overview (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf#page=80)) $500 million to $600 million more a year for about 25 years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Recent state spending on these programs The 2026 Budget Act gives $500 million for state low-income housing tax credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, the California Budget & Policy Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)) Bond money would be added to these programs over several years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Changes to how the money is split Not applicable The Legislature may move money among the listed programs “as necessary to effectively promote the development of affordable housing” (text, Sec. 54056 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Reporting Not applicable The state housing department must publish an annual report on what the bond paid for (text, Sec. 54088 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Where the $10 billion would go (text, Sec. 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)):
Program Amount
Multifamily Housing Program (rental housing; at least 10% of assisted units for extremely low income households) $5.1 billion
Supportive housing through the Multifamily Housing Program, including $150 million for youth housing $1.15 billion
Portfolio Reinvestment Program (keeping existing state-funded rentals affordable) $750 million
CalHome (homeownership and self-help housing) $600 million
CalHFA home purchase (down payment) assistance $500 million
Infill Infrastructure Grant Program $500 million
Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing $450 million
Student housing, split between UC and CSU $350 million
Buying existing unrestricted housing and adding affordability limits $200 million
Tribal Housing Grant Program $200 million
Local housing trust funds and local pilot programs (Affordable Housing Innovation Fund) $200 million
Source: Proposition 1 text, Section 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1). The separate $1.25 billion veterans bond is in the Military and Veterans Code section of the same text (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
The Legislative Analyst estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds. It would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, buy or repair homes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The measure sets no production targets of its own (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No set share for the City. The bond money goes to state programs. The Legislative Analyst says the rental programs “generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Projects in Los Angeles would compete for it statewide. The analysis does not estimate how much would reach the City.
Money cities can apply for. $200 million would be “available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The text sends it through the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program, which requires a local trust fund with its own ongoing money (text, Sec. 54054(b)(11) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Stalled projects in the region. Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit housing lender that backs Proposition 1 and gave $100,000 to the Yes campaign, counted 39,880 affordable homes statewide that had local approvals but lacked the funding to start construction at the end of 2025. It put 9,533 of them in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. It did not break out the City of Los Angeles (Enterprise report, p. 3 (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf#page=3); Yes on Prop 1 coalition list (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition)).
The City’s own housing tax. The City’s main local source of new affordable housing money is Measure ULA, the tax on property sales over $5 million. The Housing Department reported it raised nearly $1.2 billion from its start through April 30, 2026 (LAHD report, May 10, 2026 (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-0088-S1_rpt_lahd_05-10-26.pdf)). The Legislative Analyst says Proposition 1 money “would be used together with other government monies” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)).
No City tax. The state would repay the $10 billion bond from its General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Proposition 1 does not create a local tax (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
We did not find a City Council resolution or City Housing Department statement on Proposition 1 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 1 is a bond act written by the Legislature. It needed a two-thirds vote in each house and the Governor’s signature, then voter approval (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI); SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Feb. 18, 2025: SB 417 was introduced (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). Its lead authors are Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas. The principal coauthors are Sen. Christopher Cabaldon and Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 6, 2026: The Senate Housing Committee approved it 8-1 (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 27, 2026: The Senate passed it 30-9. The no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Choi, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Niello, Seyarto, Strickland and Valladares (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
April 22 and May 14, 2026: The Assembly Housing Committee (10-2) and Appropriations Committee (12-3) approved it (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly passed the amended bill 61-7, the Senate agreed 29-2, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it the same day. It became Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026 (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). The Assembly no votes were Chen, DeMaio, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Seyarto and Strickland (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a state bond law cannot take effect until it has been submitted to the people and “shall have received a majority of all the votes cast for and against it at such election” (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI)). The bond act itself says it becomes operative only if voters adopt it on Nov. 3, 2026 (text, Sec. 54051 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 1 (November 2018): a $4 billion housing and veterans bond (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 56.2% statewide and 64.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)). The Budget Center says its money was fully committed by the end of 2023 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2018): $2 billion for supportive housing for people with mental illness (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 63.4% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 1 (March 2024): a mental health bond that included $2 billion for housing for veterans and others facing homelessness (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). It passed with 50.2% statewide and 54.0% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, March 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
The argument in favor is signed by Anni Chung of Self-Help for the Elderly, Jeffery Freitas of the California Federation of Teachers and John H. Ing of US Vets (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Need: “More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.”
Veterans: $1.25 billion goes “solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership” through CalVet.
Construction: it “jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes.”

No argument against Proposition 1 was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).

Chione Flegal, executive director of Housing California, which backs the measure, told the Bay Area News Group that tens of thousands of affordable units are “shovel-ready” and that “you have both an incredible need and the conditions to actually get building quickly” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).

What would change
Today If Proposition 1 passes
State housing bond money The 2018 housing bond has been spent. The last voter-approved housing money was $2 billion in the 2024 mental health bond (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm); LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)) $10 billion in new general obligation bonds for housing programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Veterans home loans (CalVet) Last funded by a $1 billion bond in 2018 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)) $1.25 billion more, repaid by veterans’ mortgage payments (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
State budget About $6 billion a year goes to repay bonds, about 3% of General Fund revenue (LAO bond overview (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf#page=80)) $500 million to $600 million more a year for about 25 years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Recent state spending on these programs The 2026 Budget Act gives $500 million for state low-income housing tax credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, the California Budget & Policy Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)) Bond money would be added to these programs over several years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Changes to how the money is split Not applicable The Legislature may move money among the listed programs “as necessary to effectively promote the development of affordable housing” (text, Sec. 54056 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Reporting Not applicable The state housing department must publish an annual report on what the bond paid for (text, Sec. 54088 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Where the $10 billion would go (text, Sec. 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)):
Program Amount
Multifamily Housing Program (rental housing; at least 10% of assisted units for extremely low income households) $5.1 billion
Supportive housing through the Multifamily Housing Program, including $150 million for youth housing $1.15 billion
Portfolio Reinvestment Program (keeping existing state-funded rentals affordable) $750 million
CalHome (homeownership and self-help housing) $600 million
CalHFA home purchase (down payment) assistance $500 million
Infill Infrastructure Grant Program $500 million
Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing $450 million
Student housing, split between UC and CSU $350 million
Buying existing unrestricted housing and adding affordability limits $200 million
Tribal Housing Grant Program $200 million
Local housing trust funds and local pilot programs (Affordable Housing Innovation Fund) $200 million
Source: Proposition 1 text, Section 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1). The separate $1.25 billion veterans bond is in the Military and Veterans Code section of the same text (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
The Legislative Analyst estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds. It would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, buy or repair homes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The measure sets no production targets of its own (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No set share for the City. The bond money goes to state programs. The Legislative Analyst says the rental programs “generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Projects in Los Angeles would compete for it statewide. The analysis does not estimate how much would reach the City.
Money cities can apply for. $200 million would be “available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The text sends it through the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program, which requires a local trust fund with its own ongoing money (text, Sec. 54054(b)(11) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Stalled projects in the region. Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit housing lender that backs Proposition 1 and gave $100,000 to the Yes campaign, counted 39,880 affordable homes statewide that had local approvals but lacked the funding to start construction at the end of 2025. It put 9,533 of them in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. It did not break out the City of Los Angeles (Enterprise report, p. 3 (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf#page=3); Yes on Prop 1 coalition list (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition)).
The City’s own housing tax. The City’s main local source of new affordable housing money is Measure ULA, the tax on property sales over $5 million. The Housing Department reported it raised nearly $1.2 billion from its start through April 30, 2026 (LAHD report, May 10, 2026 (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-0088-S1_rpt_lahd_05-10-26.pdf)). The Legislative Analyst says Proposition 1 money “would be used together with other government monies” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)).
No City tax. The state would repay the $10 billion bond from its General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Proposition 1 does not create a local tax (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
We did not find a City Council resolution or City Housing Department statement on Proposition 1 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 1 is a bond act written by the Legislature. It needed a two-thirds vote in each house and the Governor’s signature, then voter approval (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI); SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Feb. 18, 2025: SB 417 was introduced (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). Its lead authors are Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas. The principal coauthors are Sen. Christopher Cabaldon and Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 6, 2026: The Senate Housing Committee approved it 8-1 (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 27, 2026: The Senate passed it 30-9. The no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Choi, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Niello, Seyarto, Strickland and Valladares (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
April 22 and May 14, 2026: The Assembly Housing Committee (10-2) and Appropriations Committee (12-3) approved it (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly passed the amended bill 61-7, the Senate agreed 29-2, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it the same day. It became Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026 (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). The Assembly no votes were Chen, DeMaio, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Seyarto and Strickland (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a state bond law cannot take effect until it has been submitted to the people and “shall have received a majority of all the votes cast for and against it at such election” (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI)). The bond act itself says it becomes operative only if voters adopt it on Nov. 3, 2026 (text, Sec. 54051 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 1 (November 2018): a $4 billion housing and veterans bond (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 56.2% statewide and 64.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)). The Budget Center says its money was fully committed by the end of 2023 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2018): $2 billion for supportive housing for people with mental illness (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 63.4% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 1 (March 2024): a mental health bond that included $2 billion for housing for veterans and others facing homelessness (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). It passed with 50.2% statewide and 54.0% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, March 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
The argument in favor is signed by Anni Chung of Self-Help for the Elderly, Jeffery Freitas of the California Federation of Teachers and John H. Ing of US Vets (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Need: “More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.”
Veterans: $1.25 billion goes “solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership” through CalVet.
Construction: it “jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes.”
Taxes and oversight: “NO NEW TAXES,” with public reporting, and it “unlocks federal matching funds.”
No argument against Proposition 1 was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Chione Flegal, executive director of Housing California, which backs the measure, told the Bay Area News Group that tens of thousands of affordable units are “shovel-ready” and that “you have both an incredible need and the conditions to actually get building quickly” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says “the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest” and that bonds used for programs rather than capital projects are “a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)). Spokesperson Susan Shelley said, “The more you pile this debt on, the more difficult the budget process is” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
State Sen. Tony Strickland, who voted no, told LAist the measure has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation,” and said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)).
California YIMBY supports it and estimates the production money could build about 43,700 affordable homes. It also says the $500 million in down payment help “could drive up home prices” if housing supply does not grow (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-1-2026/)).

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | 7:48 a.m.
SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 27, 2026--
California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem — cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) — and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here:
https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/ (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261027904374/en/)
The poll results will be presented this morning to San Diego business owners at a breakfast briefing at the University Club in downtown San Diego, hosted by Quadratin California in collaboration with the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce, where AIMSA Director Jesús Javier García Ruiz will walk through the findings.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters — a community with strong ties to Mexico — at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
